newsitem.title: USA: Atlantis crew prepare for landing.
newsitem.headline: Atlantis crew prepare for landing.

text.p: NASA's space endurance champion Shannon Lucid was homeward bound on Thursday as the shuttle Atlantis fired its braking rockets for a landing in Florida.
Atlantis was scheduled to touchdown in Florida at 8:13 a.m. EDT (1213 GMT), bringing to an end the 75.2 million mile (121 million km) journey of NASA's space endurance champion.
Flying backwards off the west coast of Australia, Atlantis skipper Bill Readdy fired the shuttle's braking rockets at 7:06 a.m. EDT (1106 GMT) to begin the hour-long descent through the atmosphere.
"Looked great to us up here too, and especially Shannon," radioed Readdy as mission control confirmed a sucessful burn.
"I bet she can taste those M&Ms already," said spacecraft communicator Bill Gregory from mission control, referring to Lucid's favourite candy.
The final leg of Lucid's journey would take her across the Pacific Ocean, reaching the coast of North America above British Columbia, Canada, close to Vancouver.

The shuttle will enter U.S. airspace over North Dakota, gliding across the country, crossing the east coast of Georgia, before flying down the Florida shoreline and turning to land at Kennedy Space Centre.
On its 10-day mission, Atlantis collected Lucid from the Russian space station Mir where she had spent six months in orbit, longer than any other woman and a record for an American astronaut.

The 53-year-old mother of three was to ride home in a reclining seat to cushion her body against the tug of gravity. After six months in weightlessness, the space agency's doctors expect her to feel weak and woozy.
Flight controllers required near pristine weather conditions for the landing because of the failure of one of three auxiliary power units shortly after Atlantis reached orbit on Sept. 16.
The shuttle can land safely with just two of these devices but the loss of a second could place it in danger. Light winds and mostly clear skies were needed for Atlantis to land.
The shuttle will be met on the runway by a team of doctors, nurses and paramedics in case Lucid should require medical attention after her 188-day stay in space.
Atlantis spent five days linked to Russia's orbiting outpost. The shuttle crew transferred more than 6,000 lbs of supplies to and from the station and left behind Lucid's replacement, John Blaha.
Blaha, a 54-year-old former Vietnam veteran, is due to spend four months aboard Mir. Atlantis will return in January to retrieve him.
